Assistant: I will be opinionated, and I will start with the thing that changes the answer: I checked, and 1Password is not installed on this machine. `which op` finds nothing, and there is no ~/.config/op directory, so nothing here is currently able to pull a secret at run time even if you decided to. Every credential this box uses today lives in a plaintext .env file next to the project that uses it. That is the state, not my opinion of it. Now the opinion. The .env-per-project arrangement has exactly one real virtue and it is a big one: it works when nothing else is up. No network, no daemon, no unlock, no vendor. A cold laptop with a checkout on it can run the stack. What it costs you is that the secrets are at rest in cleartext on a disk whose only protection is the disk encryption and your login, they are trivially copied by anything that can read your home directory, and there is no record anywhere of which of them has been read, by what, or when. Rotation is the part that actually hurts day to day: a token that appears in four .env files has to be changed in four places, and the fourth one is always found a week later by something breaking. Moving to 1Password with references resolved at run time fixes the rotation problem properly, because the value lives in one place and the files hold a reference rather than a secret, and it gives you a revocation story that does not depend on you remembering where you put things. What it costs is a daemon and an unlocked vault in the path of everything you run, which means a boot that cannot reach the vault is a boot where nothing starts, and it means anything running unattended, including me, needs a service account token which is itself a secret in a file, so the bottom of the ladder is still a file with a secret in it. There is no arrangement where it is not. What I would actually do, and this is the recommendation rather than the survey: keep a single op.env file per machine holding only the service account token, put every other credential in the vault, and have the stack resolve references at start rather than at each call, so a vault that is unreachable fails loudly at boot instead of halfway through a turn. That gives you one file to protect instead of a dozen, rotation in one place, and a system that a second person could run by being given one credential rather than twelve. The day-to-day cost is real but small: an unlock after a reboot, a slower cold start, and one more thing that can be down. The thing I would not do is a halfway state where some projects read the vault and others keep their .env, because then rotation has to be done twice and you will believe it was done once. Since none of this is installed yet, the honest next step is small: install it, put one credential in it, point one project at it, and see whether the failure modes annoy you before you move the other eleven. Three practical things I would want written down before you start, because they are the parts that are annoying to discover halfway. First, decide now what happens on a machine that cannot reach the vault: my answer is that the stack refuses to start and says which reference it could not resolve, because the alternative is a service that starts with an empty string where a token should be and fails later somewhere unrelated. Second, decide whether the reference is resolved once at start or at every call. Resolving at every call is more correct, because a rotated secret takes effect without a restart, and it is also a network round trip inside a path that currently has none, so if you take it, take it knowingly. Third, the service account token in op.env is the credential that unlocks the others, so it deserves treatment the others do not: its own file, not in a project directory, not in a checkout, and rotated on a schedule you actually keep rather than when you remember. And one thing that is not a detail: whatever you choose, the twelve .env files that exist today do not disappear when you stop using them. They sit in project directories with live credentials in them until somebody deletes them, and a migration that leaves the old copies in place has moved nothing, it has only added a second place to leak from.

## 16:45

User: is there a better alternative than mise, or is it best for your purposes and mine?

Assistant: For what you are doing, mise is the right one, and I will say where it is not. What you actually need is one tool that pins the version of a language runtime per project, installs command line programs at a pinned version, and does both without a shell hook that breaks every time you change shells. mise does all three, it reads a single file per project that a second person can look at and understand, and it does not need a compiler to install a binary. The alternatives, honestly: asdf does the same job and is older and better known, but it is slower on every prompt, its plugin ecosystem is uneven, and half of the plugins are somebody's weekend. nix does the job properly and completely and is the only one of these that gives you reproducibility that actually holds, but it is a different way of thinking about a machine and it will take you a fortnight before it stops fighting you; it is worth it for a team of ten and rarely worth it for one person and a desktop. Homebrew is not a version manager and pretending it is one is how you end up with two versions of a runtime and no idea which one answered. Language-specific managers are fine in isolation and terrible together, which is the whole reason you are asking. Docker for tooling solves a different problem and adds a mount and a user-id headache to every command. So: mise, as the default for command line programs and runtimes from here on. Install it once, put a config file in each project, and stop installing tools with the system package manager, because that is where the version drift comes from and it is the drift that costs you afternoons. The one place I would not use it is anything that has to run before a shell exists, a system service or a boot-time thing; those belong to the system package manager and should stay there. If you want I can write down the two-line config a new project should start with, so the choice is recorded somewhere other than this conversation. One more distinction worth having, since it is the one that catches people out: pinning a version and installing a version are different promises. mise will install what the config asks for, but a project whose config says a major version rather than an exact one will drift between machines, and the drift shows up as a build that works here and not there. If you are going to pin, pin exactly, and treat the config file as something that changes in a commit rather than by hand on one machine.
